extracted.intended_audience: government lawyers, Department of War/Defense legal officers, and attorneys advising on federal acquisition and disposition of real property
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal rules governing how the United States may acquire, accept, hold, use, lease, condemn, and dispose of land and interests in land (especially military reservations), including required statutory authority, title approval, and limits on executive action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority required to purchase or accept land
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of the prohibition of section 3736, R. S., that 'no land shall be purchased on account of the United States, except under a law authorizing the same,' a head of department (e.g., Secretary of War) cannot accept a grant by gift of land or of an easement in land without statutory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited opinions: R. 45, 359 (June 1882); P. 40, 447 (May 1890); 43, 70 (Sept. 1890); C. 3896 (Feb. 24, 1898); 12242 (Mar. 1902). Example: purchase of lots in a city cemetery for a neighboring military post was not legal absent Congressional authority. Where Congress has expressly authorized acquisition by purchase, condemnation, or donation for specific purposes (e.g., fortifications), donations in aid of such purposes may be accepted if offending clauses (e.g., maintenance obligations) are eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority must be clear and indisputable
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory authority relied upon for the purchase of land by a head of a department should be clear and indisputable; a general appropriation for maintaining existing property does not necessarily authorize purchase of additional land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: authority to purchase additional land for interment of soldiers could not be derived from a general appropriation for maintaining existing national cemeteries. Citation: R. 4^, 50 (Nov. 1877).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statutory grants strictly construed
rubrics_metrics.description: A statute conferring a specific authority to purchase certain land should, in the exercise of the authority, be strictly construed (e.g., where statute authorized purchase of a certain described tract for a stated sum, the officer is not authorized to purchase only a portion of it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: R. 38, 346 (Oct. 1876); P. 37, 203 (Dec. 1889); C. 13580 (Nov. 4, 1902); 15110 (Sept. 1903). Exception/clarification: purchases of portions of lands authorized under an appropriation may sometimes be lawful when prices indicate the balance of appropriation will cover the remainder and acquiring portions is necessary to accomplish the appropriation's object (C. 13580, 15110, 24464).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied authority for lands needed for forts/public buildings (sec.1838) does not override title-approval rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Under implied authority (sec. 1838, R. S.), lands required as sites for forts, arsenals, or needful public buildings may be purchased or acquired by gift without state consent, but public money cannot be expended on buildings until title has been approved by the Attorney General (sec. 355 implications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney General opinions cited: 10 Op. Atty. Gen. 35; 15 id. 212. Practical effect: acquisition may occur but expenditure for construction is limited if title approval lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal acceptance of a deed not required; acceptance may be presumed
rubrics_metrics.description: No formal acceptance of a deed, apart from the delivery, is necessary; acceptance may be presumed from circumstances such as placing the deed on record, possession of the deed, beneficial conveyance to the grantee, and exercising ownership over the property conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Secretary of War received deed in 1871, land used as cemetery until 1880; later refusal to accept did not divest title because acceptance had been legally presumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eminent domain authority in States requires express Congressional legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to acquire land in a State by exercise of eminent domain (condemnation in U.S. circuit court or State courts) can be vested in an executive official of the United States only by express legislation of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: R. 42, 63 (Dec. 1878). Practical implication: executive officials lack condemnation power absent explicit statutory delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner entitled to just compensation; condemnation requires reasonable provision for obtaining compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution provides private property shall not be taken 'for public use without just compensation.' It does not require compensation be actually paid in advance, but the owner is entitled to reasonable, certain, and adequate provision for obtaining compensation before his occupancy is disturbed. Where there is no provision for compensation, property should not be taken against owner’s consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: condemnation proceedings adjoining the Presidio of San Francisco should not be instituted prior to an appropriation by Congress (cited authorities: a 3231, May 1907; 20561, Oct. 26, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts are not agents of U.S. for condemnation unless authorized by Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general act making State courts an agency of the United States for the purpose of condemning lands; proceedings should be had in a United States court under an act of Congress, or in a State court when such court has by act of Congress been made an agency for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: P. 38, 271 (Feb. 1890). Practical effect: condemnation venue depends on Congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where statute requires 'acquire the title' strict compliance — contracts granting joint use do not satisfy
rubrics_metrics.description: When an enactment requires the Secretary to 'acquire the title' to certain lands sufficient for a right-of-way (e.g., for a canal), a contract granting joint use with a railroad company was not compliance; if no better title can be obtained by agreement, the Secretary should proceed to condemnation as authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: P. 51, 184 (Jan. 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney General's written approval of title required before expending public money on certain military sites (section 355)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 355 R.S. prohibits expenditure of public money upon any site of land purchased for military purposes (inter alia) 'until the written opinion of the Attorney General shall be had in favor of the validity of the title.' Before payment can be made for land acquired by purchase, condemnation, or donation, the title must be approved by the Attorney General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C. 12154 (Mar. 31, 1902); 15611 (Dec. 15, 1903). Exception/limitation: in practice, appropriations have been used to erect temporary shelter on insular lands or for temporary purposes without first acquiring title, and section 355 has been held not to apply in some such cases (C. 12347; 13680).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenses incident to purchase (abstracts, surveys) properly chargeable to appropriation for property when purchase intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the land is to be purchased, the expense of procuring an abstract of title and expense of survey are proper charges against the appropriation for the property. If abstracts were procured when it was intended to purchase but condemnation later occurred, those abstract expenses are not part of condemnation expenses and are payable from the appropriation for the property; expenses of serving offers in condemnation are part of condemnation costs and cannot be paid from the appropriation for the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title assurance requires proper certification — county record custodian, not the abstracting attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: The title to lands purchased on account of the United States is not properly assured by a certificate of 'no liens' signed by the attorney who made the abstract; the proper person to make such a certificate is the custodian of the records of judgments and other record liens in the county where the land is located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: P. 83, 292 (July 1889). Practical guidance: obtain official certificates from record custodian rather than relying solely on counsel's 'no liens' certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling vendor's lien or encumbrance: practical safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Attorney General certified title subject to a vendor's lien for purchase money and the lienholder could not be located, it was advised that the conveyance be accepted but secured by a certified check in the amount of the deed; where title was encumbered by a judgment lien and appeal pending, agreement to withhold part of the purchase price until removal of the lien was legally permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C. 21021 (Dec. 1906); C. 26834 (June 6, 1910). Practical guidance: use escrow/withholding arrangements or certified funds to protect government interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on enlarging purchase price after lump-sum acquisition or recovering for acreage shortage
rubrics_metrics.description: Where part of a tract was purchased for a lump consideration described as containing '150 acres, more or less' and later more acreage was found, the Secretary could not legally add to the purchase price to procure the addition (this would amount to satisfying a claim). Where lands were purchased in gross and a later survey showed shortage of acreage, absent fraud the United States could not recover for the shortfall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C. 9469 (Jan. 3, 1901); C. 24464 (Sept. 5 and 23, 1911). Practical implication: lump-sum purchases generally stand; buy-by-acre agreements differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-limited reservations or rights (e.g., timber removal) expire with the time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Where lands conveyed to the United States contained a reservation of the right to cut and remove timber within a stated time, and the grantor sought an extension after expiration, the rights under the reservation expired with the time limit and the uncut timber became property of the United States; the Secretary could not legally grant the extension after expiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: C. 21027 (Sept. 27, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition of easements vs. fee: AG opinion not always required; department's determination final for accounting officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no lands are purchased but only an easement is acquired (or a leasehold interest), or where the purchase is not for erection of structures described in section 355, the Attorney General's opinion is not required by law; the decision of the proper department as to sufficiency of title for its purposes is not subject to review by accounting officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C. 11585 (Nov. 30, 1907); C. 22661 (Jan. 25, 1908). Example: donation to U.S. of perpetual easement for a levee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromise authority: Attorney General can compromise suits and accept partial conveyances to United States
rubrics_metrics.description: In a suit regarding title to lands claimed as a military reservation, the Attorney General, under his power to compromise the suit, may consent to a decree by which title to a portion of the premises is adjudged to the United States and title to another portion to the defendants; such procedure is not contrary to section 3736 and does not require special Congressional authority to accept conveyance of the awarded portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: C. 25778 (Aug. 4, 1910). Practical effect: AG compromise can secure partial acquisition without separate statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint resolutions authorizing temporary emergency works may be treated as permanent legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint Resolution No. 18 (Apr. 11, 1898) providing for erection of a temporary fort or fortification in case of emergency, with consent of owner and without compliance with section 355 R.S., has been regarded as permanent legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: C. 15611 (Feb. 21, 1908). Practical implication: specific legislative measures for emergencies can carry lasting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress has exclusive power to dispose of U.S. property; executive cannot alienate absent authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution vests in Congress the exclusive power to dispose of the property of the United States, real or personal; the Secretary of War, in the absence of authority from Congress, cannot alienate land of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples: P. 29, 259 (Jan. 1889); C. 13074 (Aug. 19, 1902); 14454 (Apr. 17, 1903); 19896 (June 16, 1906). Practical effect: executive proposals to substitute private improvements or to alienate property without statute are invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive officers should not decide or surrender disputed titles to public lands — courts decide
rubrics_metrics.description: Where title to a portion of land acquired for a military reservation is disputed by a private individual, the Secretary of War has no jurisdiction to pass upon and decide such a question or to surrender such portion; questions of whether the United States has title are for the courts to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: P. 62, 442; 63, 90 (Bee, 1893); C. 19896 (June 16, 1906). Practical implication: litigation, not unilateral executive action, resolves competing title claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory grants equivalent to patents; conditions precedent create title upon performance without deed
rubrics_metrics.description: A statute may grant title and a statutory grant is equivalent to a patent — the highest form of title; where a grant by statute is made upon a condition precedent, upon performance the title becomes complete without any written deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: R. 37, 696 (June 1876); R. 36, 130 (Dec. 1874). Example: act vesting title to a railroad company upon filing/locating route; no deed necessary after conditions performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of grant matter: 'cede' implies simple absolute grant without additional covenants
rubrics_metrics.description: When an act of Congress authorized the Secretary to 'cede' certain piers to a city, the term 'cede' called for a simple absolute grant; the Secretary was not empowered to attach covenants or conditions as to use or care of the piers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: R. 53, 381 (Apr. 1887). Practical guidance: the form of Congressional language dictates permitted terms in conveyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deeds purporting to effect statutorily-prescribed sales should recite compliance with statutory procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an act of Congress authorized and directed sale of a parcel of land at public auction and prescribed manner of advertising, the deed should preferably contain recitals showing that the provisions of the act under which it was given were complied with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: C. 631 (Nov. 1894). Practical implication: include recitals evidencing statutory compliance to ensure conveyance validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse possession/prescription does not run against the sovereign; statutes of limitation not binding on U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: It is well settled that adverse possession cannot give title as against the Government; while the United States may avail itself of statutes of limitation, it is not bound thereby. Thus long continued occupancy by private parties gives them no title against U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C. 1069 (Mar. 13, 1895); C. 9003 (Oct. 3, 1900); authorities cited (Lindsey v. Miller, Jordan v. Barrett, etc.). Practical effect: claims by prescription against government lands generally fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for trespass and conduct during litigation — injunctions and limits on military force
rubrics_metrics.description: Title and possession of U.S. lands should be protected by appropriate remedies (e.g., injunction for continuous trespass); an officer or agent sued in court should appear and answer rather than employ physical force to resist process, and military force employed to protect possession should not obstruct judicial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: injunction for continuous trespass on Washington Aqueduct lands; instruction to commandant to give trespassers reasonable notice to quit and remove them if they do not comply (R. ^2, 256; C. 12941; 16983). Citation: P. 52, 182 (Feb. 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchase bounded by streets/highways gives fee to center unless excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the general rule, the purchase of land bounded by streets or highways gives title to the fee to the center of the street or highway where such title is in the grantor, unless the conveyance excludes the street or highway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: where title to lots of a subdivision was acquired for enlargement of a military reservation, on vacation of streets within the reservation the fee to center passes to the United States unless excluded by conveyance language.
